lines: Your first real job offer will come with a benefits packet, and somewhere in it is a line about a 401(k) and a match. Over a career, that one line can be worth hundreds of thousands of dollars.

A 401(k) is a retirement account through your job. You pick a percent of pay, and that slice of every paycheck goes in and gets invested before you ever see it. In 2026 you can put in up to 24,500 dollars a year.

Many employers add a match. If yours matches 100 percent up to 4 percent of pay, and you earn 50,000 dollars, you put in 2,000 and they add 2,000. That's a 100 percent return on day one. Always put in at least enough to get the whole match.
The match may need to vest, which means become fully yours, after a few years on the job. Your own contributions are always yours.

Traditional accounts skip the tax now and tax the money when you take it out. Roth accounts are the reverse: you pay tax now, and everything comes out tax-free in retirement. If your tax rate is low now and likely higher later, Roth usually wins. If the rates are the same, they tie exactly.

An IRA is a retirement account you open yourself, at a brokerage like Oakline. In 2026 you can put in up to 7,500 dollars, but no more than you earned from work. A summer job is enough to start a Roth IRA in college.
Time does the heavy lifting. 200 dollars a month from age 22, growing 7 percent a year after inflation, is about 686,000 dollars at 67. Start at 32 instead and it's about 332,000, less than half.
Don't cash out early. Before age 59 and a half, you usually pay a 10 percent penalty plus income tax. When you change jobs, roll the money into an IRA or your new plan instead.

The order is simple: get the whole match, then fill a Roth IRA, then put more in the 401(k), all in low-cost index or target-date funds. Like a squirrel burying acorns, put a little away with every paycheck and leave it alone. The ones left in the ground grow into oaks.
